lead: The Converse-Wood-Smith technique is an ear-pinning (otoplasty) method that creates or sharpens the antihelix, the inner fold of the ear, by making two full-thickness incisions in the cartilage parallel to the desired fold and shaping it with tubing sutures.[1] People have it to bring protruding or poorly folded ears closer to the head and give them a natural contour, which changes how prominent the ears look from the front and side.

Wikipedia describes it as a refinement of the earlier Luckett approach, whose single incision produced a fold that looked sharp and unnatural, and records that Converse described a technique for lop ears in 1955.[1] It belongs to the cartilage-cutting family of otoplasty methods (Wikipedia's Group II), alongside Chongchet-Stenstrom, and contrasts with suture-only approaches such as Mustarde's technique.[1]

Published experience with Converse-type methods includes a 1976 German review of 77 patients operated with a modified Converse technique, and a 2004 report in Facial Plastic Surgery of a modified Converse technique in 210 patients with protruding ears, combining a posterior incomplete cartilage incision with permanent sutures and cavum rotation.[5][2]

angle.text: The operation reshapes ear cartilage so the antihelix is defined and the ear no longer projects outward. Patients seek it so their ears look proportionate and are less noticeable.

paras: Two full-thickness incisions run parallel to the desired antihelical fold, and tubing sutures shape the cartilage into the new fold.[1] Wikipedia lists the aesthetic goals of otoplasty in general: from the front the helical rim should be visible but not hidden behind the antihelix, from behind it should be straight rather than C-shaped, and from the side the contour should look soft rather than sharp.[1]

The 2004 modified version used a posterior incomplete incision, permanent sutures and cavum rotation when needed, and the authors reported a good anterior width and normal relief, with a shaped antihelix and superior crus.[2] Otoplasty may be done under local anaesthesia, local with sedation, or general anaesthesia, and Wikipedia describes timing as around age four for pronounced prominence in children, with the ear near adult size by about age six.[1]

Wikipedia traces ear surgery back to the Sushruta Samhita (about 500 AD). Johann Friedrich Dieffenbach described cartilage excision and suturing to the mastoid in 1845, and Edward Talbott Ely performed an ear pinback in New York in 1881.[1] The Luckett procedure used a single full-thickness incision to fold the antihelix; Converse and Wood-Smith are credited with a two-incision technique producing a more natural fold, and Converse described a lop-ear technique in 1955.[1] Mustarde (1963) and Stenstrom (1963) and Furnas (1968) followed with suture and abrasion approaches.[1]

Mustarde (1963) uses mattress sutures on exposed cartilage without cutting it, Furnas (1968) uses concha-mastoid sutures to reduce the angle between the concha and the mastoid, and the Merck stitch method is closed and minimally invasive.[1] Surgeons have noted that cartilage-cutting methods carry risks of hematoma, skin necrosis and ear deformity, which has led to growing use of cartilage-sparing and suture-based methods.[4]

The 1976 HNO review followed 77 patients with unilateral or bilateral otoplasty between six months and five years after a modified Converse operation, comparing objective results with patient satisfaction. It classed 64.9 percent as good, 31.2 percent as showing only some improvement and 3.9 percent as failures suggesting reoperation, with an average helix to mastoid distance of 18.8 mm in the upper-middle third and 18.0 mm in the middle-lower third in the good results.[5] The 2004 series of 210 patients reported a shaped antihelix and good anterior width.[2]

Wikipedia lists hematoma, infection (including perichondritis), suture extrusion and overcorrection or an unnatural contour among otoplasty risks, and describes a soft dressing for several days followed by a loose headband at night for three to six weeks, with swelling and bruising settling within about two weeks.[1] It describes hematoma as needing prompt evacuation, suture extrusion as the most common complication and overcorrection or unnatural contour as the most common significant one.[1]

A rabbit study compared three antihelical-fold otoplasty techniques in 18 animals and examined new cartilage growth and whether recurrence related to the method or to how long sutures held the fold.[3]

A 1976 retrospective review of 77 patients and a 2004 case series of 210 patients with protruding ears reported on modified Converse techniques, the latter combined with cavum rotation.[5][2] A 1994 rabbit study compared otoplasty techniques histologically.[3] No randomized trials of the Converse technique were found.

name: Converse–Wood-Smith otoplasty

card.summary: A cartilage-cutting ear-pinning method using parallel full-thickness incisions to build a fold; older, with little modern human data located.
card.note: Cartilage-cutting methods are described as carrying higher hematoma and deformity risk.

quick.overview:
This otoplasty cuts through ear cartilage in parallel lines and uses tubing sutures so the cartilage forms an antihelical fold. It stems from Converse's 1955 work.

Only animal research and general descriptions were found.
quick.mechanism: Full-thickness cartilage incisions let it bend into a fold held by sutures.
quick.risks: Surgeons report hematoma, skin necrosis and ear deformity concerns with cartilage-cutting methods, which contributed to a shift toward suture-only techniques.
